youtube.baslik: Case: Speech Delay and Flat Tympanograms in a Toddler | Lesson 289 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
In a fictional case we evaluate a three-year-old with delayed speech: otoscopy, type B tympanograms and ear canal volume, conditioned play audiometry with masked bone conduction, fluctuating hearing and language development in otitis media with effusion, teamwork with the ENT physician and the speech-language pathologist, and the check after ear tubes.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Rosenfeld et al., Clinical Practice Guideline: Otitis Media with Effusion (Update), Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, 2016; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Northern and Downs, Hearing in Children.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we evaluate, step by step, a three-year-old with delayed speech and flat tympanograms.
We will cover play audiometry and tympanometry, how a fluctuating conductive loss affects language, and teamwork.
Our case is entirely fictional: a three-year-old is brought in because of concern that speech is delayed.
According to the family, the child uses about twenty words and does not yet combine words into sentences.
The child has attended day care for a year and has frequent colds; there have also been a few earaches.
The family says the child sometimes does not turn when called, turns up the TV, and hears better on some days.
The child passed newborn hearing screening in both ears, so the family did not suspect hearing.
The pregnancy and birth history is unremarkable; there is no family history of childhood-onset hearing loss.
Most three-year-olds use hundreds of words.
At this age, most children form sentences of three or more words.
Most of their speech is understood even by people who do not know the family.
This child's language is clearly below that expectation, so assessing hearing is one of the first steps.
Families sometimes blame a delay on the child's inattention or stubbornness, yet inconsistent hearing can cause similar behavior.
The assessment starts with otoscopy; the child sits on the mother's lap.
Both ear canals are clear, with no wax impaction.
Behind the tympanic membrane, an amber appearance and a thin air-fluid level can be seen.
The light reflex is not clear; this appearance suggests fluid in the middle ear.
In the report, we describe the otoscopic finding as an appearance, without making a diagnosis.
In a three-year-old, the routine two hundred twenty six hertz probe tone is used.
The tympanogram is flat in both ears, with no clear peak; in other words, type B.
Ear canal volume is within the normal range for age in both ears, for example zero point six milliliters.
A flat curve with normal volume is consistent with fluid behind an intact eardrum.
A very large volume would suggest a perforation or an open tube; a very small one, the probe tip resting against the canal wall.

cumleler.yazi: The child is developmentally ready for conditioned play audiometry, or CPA, and quickly learns to drop a block in a bucket at each sound.
cumleler.ses: The child is developmentally ready for conditioned play audiometry, or C P A, and quickly learns to drop a block in a bucket at each sound.

cumleler: The child accepts insert earphones, so each ear can be tested separately.
First, the most critical frequencies, two thousand and five hundred hertz, are tested in both ears, then one thousand and four thousand.
Bone conduction is measured, and since there is an air-bone gap, the opposite ear is masked.

cumleler.yazi: Finally, the speech recognition threshold, or SRT, is found by having the child point to a picture of the word heard.
cumleler.ses: Finally, the speech recognition threshold, or S R T, is found by having the child point to a picture of the word heard.

cumleler: The session is kept short; when the child starts to lose interest, the game is changed and response reliability is noted.
In the right ear, air conduction thresholds are between thirty and thirty five decibels HL.
In the left ear, air conduction thresholds are between thirty and forty decibels HL.
Right bone conduction was measured with the left ear masked; thresholds are normal, between ten and fifteen decibels.
Left bone conduction was also measured with the right ear masked and is within normal limits.
Both ears show an air-bone gap of twenty to thirty decibels; the picture is consistent with a mild bilateral conductive loss.
This child played along well; masking is not always possible, and then unmasked bone conduction shows only the better cochlea.

maddeler.metin: SRT: 35 dB HL in both ears
Harder in noise and at distance

cumleler: The speech recognition threshold found by picture pointing is thirty five decibels HL in both ears.
This value agrees with the pure-tone averages, which supports the reliability of the results.
As the speech banana shows, with a loss at this level, soft consonants such as s, f and t can be missed.
Noise at day care and distance from the talker make this difficulty clearly worse.
The child hears speech, but may not hear its details consistently.
Otoscopy shows an appearance suggesting fluid behind the eardrum in both ears.
The tympanograms are flat and ear canal volume is normal.
The audiogram shows normal bone conduction and a mild conductive loss in both ears.
These findings are consistent with otitis media with effusion, or OME; diagnosis and treatment decisions belong to the ENT physician.
Because the child has a speech delay, the child is referred to the ENT physician with the findings, without waiting.
In otitis media with effusion, the loss is not stable; it changes over weeks with the amount and thickness of the fluid.
In the example course on the graph, the average threshold sometimes nears normal and sometimes reaches thirty five decibels.
For the child, this means hearing the same word clearly one day and partly the next; the auditory input is inconsistent.
When fluid lasts for months, this inconsistency overlaps with the period of rapid language growth.
Most studies have not clearly shown lasting language effects in healthy children, but children with speech delay are considered at risk.
This is why guidelines recommend age-appropriate hearing testing in at-risk children, whatever the duration of fluid.
The ENT physician evaluates the middle ear fluid and decides on treatment, such as watchful waiting or ventilation tubes.
The child is also referred to a speech-language pathologist, who assesses the degree and type of language delay.
Middle ear fluid may not be the only cause of the speech delay; developmental and language causes must also be explored.
The audiologist monitors hearing while the fluid persists and after treatment, and shares the results with the team.
The family and the day care teacher are part of the team in improving the child's daily listening conditions.

maddeler.metin: Turn off the TV, reduce noise

cumleler: The family is advised to come close and face the child when talking; lip and facial cues support understanding.
Turning off the TV and reducing background noise while talking makes faintly heard consonants more accessible.
Short, clear sentences, repeated when needed, help the child catch the words.
The day care teacher is advised to seat the child nearby and to give instructions face to face.
These tips do not replace treatment, but they improve the quality of the speech the child hears while the fluid persists.

sahneler.metin: Passing a screening does not rule out a later loss. Assess hearing in every child with delayed speech.
cumleler: A clinical tip: passing newborn screening does not rule out later middle ear fluid or a late-onset loss.
In every child with delayed speech, hearing should be assessed with an age-appropriate method.
Seeing a flat tympanogram and saying only fluid is not enough; a sensorineural loss can hide beneath the fluid.
So try to measure bone conduction, and retest hearing after the fluid resolves.
At the check three months later, the fluid persists in both ears and the thresholds are similar.
The ENT physician decides to place ventilation tubes in both ears.
One month after the tubes, air conduction thresholds in both ears fall to ten to fifteen decibels HL.
The tympanogram is still flat, but ear canal volume is now large, which shows that the tube is open.
Without the volume information, the same flat curve could have been misread.
Even with hearing back to normal, language development continues to be monitored and supported with language therapy.
Example report language: reliable responses were obtained with conditioned play audiometry, using insert earphones.
Mild conductive loss between thirty and forty decibels HL in both ears; masked bone conduction is normal.
Type B tympanograms in both ears with normal ear canal volume; otoscopy shows an amber appearance behind the eardrum.
Due to speech delay, ENT and speech-language pathology evaluations are recommended; a hearing check is planned within three months.
The report is also explained to the family in plain words, and the date of the next test is given in writing.
In a child with delayed speech, hearing is assessed with an age-appropriate method, even after a passed screening.
A type B tympanogram is read together with ear canal volume; normal volume fits fluid behind an intact eardrum.
In otitis media with effusion, the loss is mild but fluctuating; in an at-risk child, hearing is tested without waiting.
The ENT physician, the speech-language pathologist, the audiologist and the family work together; treatment is the physician's decision.

sahneler.aciklama: A large volume shows the measurement _includes the middle ear_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: what does a flat tympanogram with a very large ear canal volume suggest?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: an open ventilation tube or a perforation.
A flat curve with normal volume fits fluid; a flat curve with small volume fits wax impaction or a blocked probe tip.
